doc.title: Buster Williams interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 6, 2002

title: What makes a standard: playing contemporaries' music and lyrics
summary: He argues musicians should play each other's compositions, notes the value of lyrics, and mentions upcoming projects with singers.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yeah right. It’ll do slightly better. Is there anybody that you’re aware of writing — hopefully it’s you maybe — what will become the standards.

Yeah. You know a friend of mine, we were just talking about that the other day. One of the things that Herbie Hancock and Wayne Shorter and Ron Carter, since when you’re talking about Herbie and Wayne and Ron, you know you don’t have to use their last names, everybody knows who you’re talking about. One of the things that perpetrated their music was the fact that they played each other’s music. And that’s sort of the kind of thing that Bird and Monk and Miles and Dizzy, they did also. They played each other’s music, which is what we need to do more of. We need to play more of our contemporaries’ music. And that helps make the music standards. A lot of the standards that we call standards now came from plays, or came from movies, but a standard is never a standard if it’s only played once. It’s got to be played over and over again in different kind of situations. And that’s what makes it a standard. And I mean I’d like to see more of our music, meaning the jazz compositions, becoming standard material. I guess what helps is the kind of genres that it’s played in, the kind of situations that the music is used for.
I think it helps too if there’s a lyric. © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-
It always helps if there’s a lyric.
Yeah. People can put the lyric in your head as you’re hearing it.
People like to sing these songs that they like. I’m doing a project for this summer, I’m going out with a singer named Melissa Walker. You know Melissa Walker?

She’s a very good singer. And she wants me to write music that fits her in. And a couple of years back I did a project for a Japanese singer and I wrote these songs and I wrote lyrics. And that was the first time I wrote lyrics. And they came out really good. So it’s another challenge that I have in front of me, to write these songs with lyrics. And as you said it stands a better chance of something becoming more standard material.
